part_title: IAM Password Policies, MFA, Service Roles and Identity Center

scenes.title: IAM password policy
scenes.narration: The first path shows an IAM user signing in to the AWS Console. Passwords travel over HTTPS, and the authentication service verifies the credentials against the account's configured controls. The settings panel lists typical password-policy choices: minimum length, required character categories, password reuse prevention, expiration periods and whether users can change their own passwords. The lower branch contrasts access granted with a failed or incomplete password-policy requirement. One important distinction is that changing an account password policy usually affects creation or replacement of IAM user passwords; it does not mean every sign-in simply reevaluates the entered password against new complexity rules. Existing password validity and expiry are handled by AWS authentication state. For human access, favour centralised federation through IAM Identity Center when possible, and require strong MFA as a separate security layer. Complexity alone isn't enough to prevent password reuse, credential stuffing or phishing. Configure a policy suitable for your organisation, test recovery paths and avoid long-lived programmatic access keys for IAM users.

scenes.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
scenes.narration: This slide begins with the two-factor principle: one factor is something you know, such as a password, and the second is something you have or are. The diagram then shows access granted only after the required factors are successfully verified. Compare the second-factor options across the bottom. A virtual authenticator generates time-based one-time passcodes on a phone. A physical security key can use a standards-based challenge-response mechanism over USB or NFC and, when properly configured, offers phishing-resistant authentication. A hardware token can display a rotating code without requiring an app on the phone. These methods are not equally resistant to real-world attacks. Passcodes may be phished or relayed; FIDO security keys bind authentication to the correct site more strongly. For privileged AWS access, require MFA and plan how to recover safely if a device is lost. MFA protects the login process, while IAM least privilege still determines what the authenticated principal can do. Avoid confusing stronger authentication with authorisation to every resource.

scenes.title: IAM roles for AWS services
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates how an AWS Lambda function can use an IAM execution role instead of storing an access key. Start with Lambda's service identity on the left, then follow the role-assumption path into AWS Security Token Service. The trust policy says which service principal is allowed to assume the role, while the permissions policy defines the actions that the resulting role credentials permit. The temporary session has an access key, secret access key, session token and expiration, but the function normally receives this context automatically from its execution environment. On the right, the role uses those permissions to call Bedrock and S3. Trust and permission policies solve different problems: the first enables the service to obtain the role, and the second grants access to resources. Neither should be excessively broad. In a production Lambda architecture, grant only the required Bedrock model invocation and S3 object actions, and avoid writing credentials to logs. Using a role means credentials rotate automatically and expire, reducing the risk from long-lived embedded keys.

scenes.title: IAM Identity Center login flow
scenes.narration: Follow the employee sign-in from left to right. The user opens the IAM Identity Center portal and authenticates with a configured identity source such as an enterprise directory or SAML identity provider. After authentication, the portal displays the AWS accounts and permission sets assigned to that user. The employee chooses an account and role-like access level, and Identity Center provides a temporary console session with the effective permissions. The middle examples include administrator, power-user, read-only and custom permission sets. These are assignments, not permanent administrator credentials stored in every account. The identity source manages authentication, Identity Center maps people and groups to AWS account assignments, and the permission set defines the permitted actions when a session is created. For a security architect, the important controls are centralised group membership, MFA at the correct authentication point, least-privilege permission sets and audit records. Removing an assignment stops future access, though active sessions may remain valid until their expiration. This flow simplifies access governance across many accounts.

scenes.title: IAM Identity Center across AWS Organizations
scenes.narration: This architecture shows AWS Organizations managing several separate member accounts, while IAM Identity Center centrally manages human access. Follow the left side: employees belong to groups such as DevOps, operations or auditors. Each group receives an account assignment and a permission set. On the right, a development account might grant a Developer permission set, a staging account might grant PowerUser permissions to a different team, and production might offer read-only audit access. The actual IAM roles used for access are provisioned into the assigned accounts. Notice the account isolation: permission in development does not automatically provide access to production. One person can be assigned different permission sets in different accounts, reflecting business responsibilities. The benefit is consistency without collapsing every environment into one broad identity. During onboarding, review the group, account and permission set together; during offboarding, revoke centrally managed access and review existing sessions. Organisations supplies the account structure, while Identity Center provides the workforce access layer. That's the boundary this diagram is teaching.
